questions.analysis:
Opening question, and the one that sets whether the rest is read generously. EB4E is a housing and transit organization; a purely civil-liberties answer will not land here.

PRIOR RECORD. The District 1 incumbent, Rashi Kesarwani, has a genuine pro-housing referral record: a citywide Local Density Bonus Program referral (April 14 2026, with Tregub and Humbert), a Gilman Street rezoning referral (September 19 2023), and the plan that revived Hopkins Street and carried 7-2 on July 28-29 2026. The incumbent is not a soft target on housing, and an answer implying otherwise will read as uninformed. The available contrast is not that the incumbent blocks housing — it is that the incumbent voted with the 5-4 majority to extend the Flock automated license plate reader contract on May 7 2026 while District 1 has 739 entitled homes at North Berkeley BART that have not broken ground.

The strongest posture is to concede the incumbent's housing record implicitly by not attacking it, and to compete on delivery and on the surveillance vote instead.

questions.analysis:
Narrow, technical, and a question most candidates will answer vaguely. Specificity here is cheap differentiation.

The mechanism EB4E is pointing at: California is required by statute to adopt the most recent editions of the ICC, IAPMO and NFPA model codes each triennial cycle, then amend. Local leverage is limited and the answer should say so. Berkeley does adopt local amendments and has notable reach codes, so the honest version commits to holding Berkeley's own amendments to the same cost-transparency standard being demanded of the state.

questions.analysis:
The question names MTC's Transit Priority Policy without citing it, so the answer earns credibility by supplying the reference rather than by correcting anyone: it is Resolution 4739, adopted January 28 2026. (Resolution 4664, which circulates in some secondary write-ups of this policy, is an unrelated SB1 freight corridor fund estimate. A Seamless Bay Area post renders it as 4505. Use the primary PDF.)

What adoption actually involves, from the primary text, because it is less than the phrasing suggests. A local transit priority resolution is optional — MTC's own attachment heads that section 'OPTIONAL LOCAL TRANSIT PRIORITY RESOLUTION OR POLICY' and says right-of-way owners 'should consider' adopting one. What is mandatory is procedural: a project drawing more than $250,000 in MTC discretionary funds on a roadway with fixed-route service must be reviewed by the affected transit agencies, who have 20 business days to comment, documented through the Complete Streets Checklist. No specific treatment — bus lane, signal priority, all-door boarding — is mandated.

That gap between what the policy requires and what it is imagined to require is the opening. Committing to adopt the optional local resolution is a real commitment precisely because nothing compels it.

The Transit Priority Network does not exist yet; adoption is expected in 2027. Any claim that a named Berkeley street is on it is premature.

PRIOR RECORD. Berkeley's Transit-First Policy dates to December 2001, the Implementation Plan to March 21 2023, and the Telegraph Multimodal conceptual design to October 28 2025 (Resolution 72,014-N.S.), which includes bus-only lanes.

levers.text: Adopt the optional local transit priority resolution rather than meeting only the procedural minimum
Fund the corridor studies already scheduled in the Transit-First Implementation Plan
Shape which Berkeley corridors enter MTC's Transit Priority Network before it is adopted in 2027

questions.analysis:
Explicit YES or NO, so the answer must open with the word. Everything after is credibility.

The number that matters: AC Transit's Board adopted a contingency plan in June 2026 of $53 million, 16.4 percent of service, for implementation June 2027 if the measure fails. The 37 percent figure still circulating is a superseded 2025 number, and correcting it is worth more than repeating it. Berkeley specifics: Line F loses all weekend service; Lines 65 and 67 drop to hourly and interline.

SB 63's ballot qualification was not confirmed as of the last check — AC Transit's own June 10 2026 staff report still says 'if the regional revenue measure does not qualify.' Verify before asserting it is on the ballot.

A brief note on sales tax regressivity reads as independence to most panels and costs nothing, since the answer is still yes.

levers.text: Place Berkeley formally on record supporting the regional measure by council resolution
Campaign for the measure in District 1
Press for a less regressive long-term operating revenue source than a sales tax

questions.analysis:
Asks what the candidate has championed. The candidate has not held office, so a claimed record is checkable and will not survive.

PRIOR RECORD, and it belongs to the opponent. Hopkins Street was shelved from 2022 to 2023 after a process fraught enough that it was reported to have driven traffic planners out of city government. It was revived in April 2026 without bike lanes, and then approved with protected lanes 7-2 on July 28-29 2026 under a plan put forward by the District 1 incumbent. Walk Bike Berkeley and the Sierra Club supported it; Save Hopkins opposed. Safety record on the corridor: three fatalities and 46 pedestrian and bicycle crashes between 2011 and 2026.

Conceding this cleanly costs less than contesting it. The available pivot is San Pablo Avenue, which runs the length of West Berkeley in District 1, where AC Transit completed signal priority in 2023 and the Alameda CTC bus and bike lane project keeps slipping.

levers.text: Vote to fund and defend the Hopkins implementation through construction, where projects usually die
Advance the San Pablo Avenue corridor within Berkeley's jurisdiction
Press Alameda CTC on the San Pablo bus and bike lane schedule, which is county-led, not city-led

questions.question: Who are your top endorsers? How do you plan to win the campaign?
questions.analysis:
Straightforward campaign viability question. EB4E is assessing whether this is a real campaign before assessing whether it agrees with it.

The public financing detail is the strongest single credibility item: certified, $60 contribution cap, no corporate, business, union or PAC money at all, six-to-one match on qualifying Berkeley contributions. It answers the viability question and the independence question in one move.

Endorsements should be listed without inflation. Naming a former District 1 councilmember of 25 years is worth more to this audience than a longer list of organizations.

levers.text: None — this question is descriptive
Keep the public financing certification current, since matching funds depend on continued compliance

questions.question: Berkeley saw a lot of housing construction immediately following the pandemic, but since then, construction costs have risen. Berkeley has a large number of permitted projects in the pipeline that aren't breaking ground. What would you change to help unlock Berkeley's pipeline of housing projects and get the cranes back up over our city?

verification.claim: Berkeley has a large gap between entitled units and permitted units
verification.source: Berkeley APR staff report (2024 data) and Berkeleyside (2023 data)
verification.note: 2023: 2,224 units submitted for approval, 2,093 entitled, only 431 permitted. 2024: 2,037 units entitled, 731 permitted, 708 completed. So roughly 1,300-1,650 units per year get entitled and then do not advance to permit.

verification.claim: There is currently no housing project under construction in downtown Berkeley's core
verification.source: Berkeleyside, 'Downtown Berkeley housing construction has stalled, creating empty, blighted lots'
verification.note: Berkeleyside contacted developers behind several of downtown's biggest projects and found none planning to break ground imminently. Cleared sites sitting vacant. This is a year+ old — verify it is still true before asserting it in August 2026.

verification.claim: Causes cited for the stall are construction costs, labor supply, interest rates, and reduced bank lending / investor interest
verification.source: Berkeleyside (2025-04-04) and Berkeleyside (2024-04-19)
verification.note: Insurance costs and city fees were NOT the causes cited in the sources found. Do not assert fees as a documented cause without a source.

verification.claim: A named third-party tracker quantifies the stalled pipeline
verification.source: berkeleybuild.com 'Berkeley Housing Pipeline Analysis'
verification.note: Site claims to track ~895 projects / 5,470 units pulled from Berkeley's Accela permit system via SQL, color-coding entitled-without-permit (orange) and permitted-but-not-started (yellow). Authorship, funding, and methodology NOT verified. It is advocacy-adjacent. Useful for lead generation, not for citation without checking.

verification.claim: People's Park housing has been delayed and is not yet delivered
verification.source: SF Standard, 'The battle over People's Park is over. Berkeley hasn't yet kept its promise' (2026-08-06); Berkeleyside on new developer SAHA (2025-12-11)
verification.note: UC Berkeley found a new developer (Satellite Affordable Housing Associates) in Dec 2025 for the affordable/supportive component. Details not read in full.

quotes.text: Where downtown once buzzed with construction workers building hundreds of new apartments, today there is not a single housing project under construction in the city's core.
Just 431 units received building permits in 2023, down from 887 a year prior, a 50% drop driven by high interest rates and construction costs, which have slowed housing production nationwide.

questions.analysis:
The most technically specific question on the form, and the one where a wrong diagnosis is most visible. Berkeley entitled 2,093 units in 2023 and permitted 431; entitled 2,037 in 2024 and permitted 731.

The causes documented in the reporting are construction costs, labor supply, interest rates and tighter bank lending. City fees are NOT among the cited causes. Blaming fees is the easy pro-housing applause line and it is not supported — and it would also cut the Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee that has generated over $51 million for the Housing Trust Fund. Declining that line deliberately is a stronger answer than taking it.

North Berkeley BART is the in-district case: 739 homes, 381 affordable, entitled December 11 2024 under AB 2011, groundbreaking slipped from 2025 to 2026 to at least early 2027.

levers.text: Direct gap financing to entitled-but-stalled projects rather than opening new entitlement processes
Set terms on city-owned land where Berkeley is the landowner and can accept a lower return
Extend the ministerial, decide-the-rules-once model beyond Middle Housing
Pursue state and county gap financing, since interest rates and construction costs are outside city control

questions.question: Berkeley has had success getting housing built downtown, in student neighborhoods, and in formerly redlined neighborhoods, but it has seen precious little housing production in its wealthier districts. What would you do to increase housing production in Berkeley's wealthier neighborhoods and affirmatively further fair housing?

verification.claim: Berkeley's low-production areas are the hills and the wealthy commercial corridors (Elmwood/College, Solano, North Shattuck); production concentrates downtown, Southside, and the flats
verification.source: Berkeleyside on 2023 Housing Element commitment; Berkeleyside on zoning history; Berkeley Corridors Zoning Update project page
verification.note: The City's own Housing Element names these three corridors as the affirmatively-furthering-fair-housing rezoning commitment precisely because they are high-resource and low-production.

verification.claim: Berkeley's 1916 and 1949 zoning deliberately put single-family-only in the hills/east side and density in the flats
verification.source: Berkeleyside, 'Berkeley zoning has served for many decades to separate the poor from the rich and whites from people of color'
verification.note: Berkeley enacted the nation's first single-family zoning district (Elmwood, 1916). Good framing material, well-documented.

verification.claim: The Berkeley Hills were exempted from the Middle Housing ordinance on wildfire grounds
verification.source: City of Berkeley Middle Housing Zoning page; Berkeleyside
verification.note: Middle Housing applies to R-1, R-2, R-2A and MU-R 'excluding high fire hazard areas in the Berkeley Hills.' This is the clean answer to a Q13-style 'where does your city not build' question — and a live tension, since the exemption tracks wealth as well as fire risk.

verification.claim: Official per-council-district housing production counts exist
verification.source: Searched; not found
verification.note: Berkeley's APR reports citywide, not by council district. No city dataset of units by district located. Do NOT cite a district-level production number without finding one. Corridor-level unit-capacity estimates (below) are the closest available substitute.

verification.claim: Corridors upzoning capacity estimates: ~1,700 total — up to 146 on College, 617 on Solano, 1,036 on North Shattuck
verification.source: Berkeleyside coverage of Planning Commission action; Berkeley Corridors Zoning Update staff report
verification.note: These are the SCALED-BACK figures the Planning Commission endorsed. Darrell Owens frames the Housing Element commitment as roughly 2,000 homes, so the scaled-back version is a shortfall of ~300. Solano Avenue capacity (617) is the D1-relevant number.

quotes.text: Planning staff estimated that the version of the zoning changes the commission endorsed could result in just over 1,700 total new homes across the three avenues — up to 146 on College, 617 on Solano and 1,036 on North Shattuck.

questions.analysis:
The hardest question on the form and the one that most distinguishes a real pro-housing candidate from a cautious one. It asks a District 1 candidate to support upzoning in wealthy areas, and the honest answer costs something with constituents.

PRIOR RECORD. Berkeley enacted the nation's first single-family zoning district — Elmwood, 1916. The Housing Element names the hills and the wealthy commercial corridors as the affirmatively-furthering-fair-housing rezoning commitment precisely because they are high-resource and low-production. The Corridors Zoning Update was scaled back by the Planning Commission in May 2026 after neighborhood pressure, to roughly 1,700 units of capacity, of which Solano Avenue is 617 — the District 1 piece. Southside/Telegraph, by contrast, was upzoned November 21 2023 under Rigel Robinson with Mark Humbert to roughly 2,650 units and 16 stories, which is the comparison case for what a real upzone looks like.

The Middle Housing ordinance excludes high fire hazard areas in the Berkeley Hills. The wildfire justification is real; it also tracks wealth. Naming that tension is what a serious answer looks like.

No official per-council-district production numbers exist. Do not cite one.

levers.text: Vote for the fuller Corridors upzone including the Solano Avenue segment in District 1
Require analysis separating wildfire risk from wealth in the Middle Housing hills exemption, and apply mitigation-based standards where the fire case does not hold
Defend the position publicly to District 1 constituents, which is the actual cost of this answer

org_research: East Bay for Everyone is a YIMBY / pro-housing and pro-transit organization endorsing in East Bay municipal races. The questionnaire is housing-heavy - eight of thirteen questions are housing or land use - with a 200-word cap on every answer, so specificity matters more than length. The live Berkeley items during this endorsement window are the Corridors Zoning Update (North Shattuck, College, Solano), which the Planning Commission scaled back in May 2026 after neighborhood pressure, and SB 79, effective July 1 2026, which covers North Berkeley BART unless the city adopts an alternative plan. Both touch District 1 directly. No published EB4E criticism of specific Berkeley councilmembers was found, so the organization's positions on TOPA, encampments, or individual officeholders should not be inferred.
